What NRP Is

2

What is NRP?

  • One national Kubernetes cluster, Nautilus, for research and education
  • Operated by SDSC (UC San Diego), Nebraska–Lincoln and MGHPCC; funded by NSF
  • Hardware from 70+ institutions, on research and education networks
  • Today:
  • 536 nodes at 129 sites
  • 1,460 GPUs in 33 models; 59,352 CPU cores
  • 15 PB of raw Ceph storage
  • Free for non-commercial research and education
  • One team runs it from the OS up; campuses keep priority on what they contribute
https://dash.nrp-nautilus.io

Sites from the NRP dashboard, 10 Nov 2026

Not drawn: 8 sites in Hawaii, Guam, Korea, Brazil and Europe

How It's Built

6

The Network Underneath

  • Nodes sit in campus Science DMZs, outside campus firewalls, at 10–100 Gb/s
  • Jumbo frames: MTU 9000 between all nodes
  • Regional and national R&E networks carry the traffic
  • 54 nodes sit in 51 Internet2 locations
  • Calico builds the pod network: a VXLAN overlay, IPv4 and IPv6 (309 nodes dual-stack)

Dashed: the Calico VXLAN overlay. Pods on any node reach pods on any other node directly.

7

Policy Lives in the Cluster

  • Nodes are open to the world; Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy filters at the host, before NAT
  • Hosts in a central network set reach each other with no filtering
  • Campuses keep no per-node firewall rules; local iptables and firewalld stay off
  • Why: the node population changes every week, faster than any campus change process
From the internetWhy
22/tcpSSH, for NRP operators
443/tcpHTTPS; opened on every node by cluster policy
ICMPping, and path MTU discovery for jumbo frames
8443/tcpobject reads over HTTPS and XRootD (data caches)
8444/tcpPelican tokens, director health checks, metrics
50000–51000/tcpGridFTP data channels

The last three only on nodes that run a data cache, an origin or a Globus endpoint.

https://nrp.ai/documentation/admindocs/participating/network/
8

One Cluster, Many Sites

  • One control plane; Kubernetes 1.34
  • Topology labels on every node: region, zone (143 zones), site
  • Workloads ask for locality: spread over zones, or stay near their data
  • Mostly x86-64; 3 ARM64 nodes
  • Operated from SDSC, Nebraska–Lincoln and MGHPCC

Storage

  • Rook runs 9 Ceph clusters, one per region or large site: 14.9 PB raw
  • CephFS for shared files, RBD for block, S3 for objects
  • Linstor (DRBD) for fast replicated block storage
  • CVMFS for software; local NVMe for scratch
  • Pick the pool near your compute

How We Run It

13

Git Is the Source of Truth

An admingit push
GitLabthe repo: manifests, Helm values
Argo CDcompares git with the cluster
The clusterwhat's actually running
kubectl edita manual change: drift

self-heal: put back what git says

  • Self-hosted GitLab 19.5.4: code, issues, a container registry, CI
  • Argo CD syncs 20 applications, GitLab itself among them
  • Self-heal: a manual change is reverted to what's in git; history and review come free
  • Not everything is in Argo yet: some services are still applied by hand from their repos (kubectl diff, kubectl apply, then push)

NetBox Knows Every Node

  • NetBox 4, deployed by Argo CD from the NetBox Labs Helm chart
  • netbox-agent on every node (529 pods): privileged, host network
  • lldpd learns the switch and port each NIC is cabled to
  • The site comes from the node's netbox.io/site label
  • Alongside: Diode for ingest, and a Nornir pod for automation
Switchat the site
NRP nodenetbox-agent + lldpd

Device

17

The Agent, Up Close

netbox_agent.yaml (token left out)
netbox:  url: https://netbox-4.nrp-nautilus.ionetwork:  ignore_interfaces: (dummy.*|docker.*|tunl*|cali*|vxlan.*|lo|ibp.*|.*ifb.*)  ignore_ips: (127\.0\..*)  lldp: true  nic_id: name  primary_mac: permanentvirtual:  cluster_name: nautilusdatacenter_location:  driver: cmd:kubectl get node ${NODE_NAME} -o jsonpath=    '{.metadata.labels.netbox\.io/site}' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'inventory: true
The run loop (from the startup script)
lldpd           # start listening for LLDP# at least 30 s so LLDP has found its neighbourspause $(random_between 30 "$INITIAL_DELAY_MAX")while true; do  netbox_agent -c "$RUNTIME_CONFIG" --update-all -d &&  netbox_agent -c "$RUNTIME_CONFIG" --update-inventory -d  # a day, plus up to an hour of jitter  pause $((RUN_INTERVAL + $(random_between 0 "$RUN_JITTER")))done

Interfaces the overlay creates (cali*, vxlan*, tunl*) are ignored, so NetBox holds the physical network only.

Security

Identity

Detect

Audit

  • JupyterHub scanner: no anonymous hubs

22

Sharing GPUs Fairly

  • Contributors keep priority on their nodes: reservation taints, and Kueue with NRP's own controllers
  • Priority classes: owner, nice (−10), opportunistic (preempted first)
  • Idle GPUs go to opportunistic work, such as Open Science Grid jobs for IceCube and LIGO
  • Opportunistic work must tolerate being preempted: checkpoint, or just restart
A contributed GPU node · 8 GPUs
owneridleopportunisticowner
owneridleopportunisticowner
owneridleopportunisticowner
owneridleopportunisticowner
owneridleopportunisticowner
owneridleopportunisticowner
owneridleopportunisticowner
owneridleopportunisticowner

The owner's jobs use two GPUs; six sit idle.

Opportunistic work fills the idle GPUs, for example OSG glideins.

The owner submits more work: the scheduler preempts opportunistic pods to make room.

23

How a Node Joins

1. Rack and cablepower, cooling, a Science DMZ port, jumbo frames
2. Hand over accessIPMI, or root SSH from NRP's management address
3. NRP installsUbuntu 24.04, drivers and storage; joins Nautilus
4. Labels and policyregion, zone, site, GPU model; the central Calico policy
5. It reports into NetBox, Prometheus and the perfSONAR mesh

The site

  • Keeps an on-site contact for hands-on work
  • Sends maintenance notices; forwards warranty tickets

NRP

  • Patching, packages and host hardening
  • 24/7 monitoring and alerting; incident handling from the OS up

Then it's schedulable, yours first: owner priority for your users, idle time for everyone else.

https://nrp.ai/documentation/admindocs/participating/new-contributor-guide/

27

A Request, Step by Step

ClientOpenAI API
Envoy AI Gatewayellm.nrp-nautilus.io
AIGatewayRoutex-ai-eg-model: qwen3
InferencePoolwith an endpoint picker
llm-authext_authz over gRPC; fail closed
Rate limiteroutput tokens per token and model
vLLM pod aqueue 6 · KV cache 88%
vLLM pod bqueue 0 · KV cache 31%
vLLM pod cqueue 2 · KV cache 64%

example values

One request, five stops

The gateway is the Envoy Gateway from the ingress slide, plus its AI extension, Envoy AI Gateway. A client asks for qwen3.

1. Who are you?

The gateway sends the bearer token to an external auth service over gRPC. If auth can't answer, the request fails: fail closed.

2. Which model?

The gateway reads model from the JSON body into the x-ai-eg-model header, and an AIGatewayRoute rule matches it to a backend: here an InferencePool.

3. Which pod?

The endpoint picker scores the pool's vLLM pods by queue depth, KV-cache use and prefix-cache hits, and picks one.

4. The answer, and the bill

vLLM answers. The gateway reads the token counts from the response; the rate limiter charges output tokens to this token and model.

28

Gateway Policies

apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1kind: BackendTrafficPolicymetadata: {name: envoy-ai-gateway-nrp, namespace: nrp-llm}spec:  rateLimit:    type: Global    global:      rules:      - clientSelectors:        - headers:          - {name: authorization, type: Distinct}          - {name: x-ai-eg-model, type: Distinct}        limit: {requests: 48000, unit: Minute}        cost:          request: {from: Number, number: 1}          response:            from: Metadata            metadata: {namespace: io.envoy.ai_gateway,                       key: llm_output_token}  retry:    numRetries: 2    retryOn: {httpStatusCodes: [500, 502, 503, 504]}  healthCheck:    active: {type: HTTP, http: {path: /health}, interval: 10s,             unhealthyThreshold: 3}    passive: {consecutive5XxErrors: 2, baseEjectionTime: 30s,              maxEjectionPercent: 50}

Rate limit: 48,000 output tokens a minute, per token and model

Retries: twice, on 5xx

Health: probe /health every 10 s; eject a pod after two 5xx

What a client sees (demo, 10 Nov)

$ curl -si https://ellm.nrp-nautilus.io/v1/chat/completions \    -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \    -d '{"model": "qwen3", ...}' | grep -i ratelimitx-ratelimit-limit: 48000, 48000;w=60x-ratelimit-remaining: 47999x-ratelimit-reset: 9

30

Serving with vLLM

qwen3, from the cluster (shortened)
apiVersion: apps/v1kind: StatefulSetmetadata: {name: qwen38-flash-next-a100, namespace: nrp-llm}spec:  replicas: 2  template:    metadata:      labels: {component: llm, service-group: qwen-vllm-inference}    spec:      priorityClassName: owner          # tolerates the reservation taint      containers:      - image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0        args: ["vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 --port 5000                --tensor-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel                --enable-prefix-caching --max-model-len 1000000                --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 --otlp-traces-endpoint ..."]        resources:          limits: {cpu: "36", memory: 440Gi, nvidia.com/a100: 4}        readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /health, port: 5000}}      affinity:   # GPU memory > 80 GB, Ampere or newer  volumeClaimTemplates:  - metadata: {name: qwen38-flash-cache}    spec: {storageClassName: linstor-igrok,           resources: {requests: {storage: 256Gi}}}

Labels put the pod in the qwen3 pool; priority owner

vLLM: tensor parallel 4, expert parallel, prefix caching, traces to OpenTelemetry

Health: probes on /health; vLLM and DCGM metrics go to the same Prometheus and Thanos, and drive the LLM status page

Weights on a Linstor volume, so a restart doesn't download them again

16 servers like this. Their config is in GitLab (prp/llm-proxy), applied by hand, not yet by Argo CD

31

Borrowing Idle GPUs

  • Extra replicas run at opportunistic priority on idle GPUs and join the same pool
  • qwen3-small: 4 × A6000 at Chico State as owner, plus two H200 replicas at Fresno State as opportunistic
  • glm-5 and gemma borrow H100s and A100s at low priority too
  • Preempted when the owner needs the GPU; the endpoint picker routes around the gap
InferencePool qwen3-smallselects pods by label: service-group=qwen3-small

  • DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, two copies
  • Head and worker StatefulSets

  • NCCL settings pinned, e.g. NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0

Expert parallelism spreads the model's experts across the GPUs. Both copies run on SDSC's Expanse H100 nodes.

Guardrails

  • RBAC denies secrets, exec and every write
  • Namespace allowlist; credentials redacted
  • Logs and events treated as untrusted (prompt injection)
  • Budgets on tool calls, iterations and time

Status

  • Phase 1, read-only: built and tested with mocks
  • Phase 2, write actions behind two-human approval: not started
  • Also an MCP server, and an eval harness to compare models

Ways to Run Work

Interactive: JupyterHub

  • Pick a GPU from the start menu; explore, debug, teach
  • Idle servers stop: 1 hour after you close the browser on NRP's hub, 6 hours at most on any hub

Interactive: a pod

  • Start a container with kubectl, then open a shell in it
  • Deleted after 6 hours; at most 2 GPUs

Long-running: a Deployment

  • Keeps a service up (a web app, a database) and restarts it if it crashes
  • Removed after 2 weeks unless admins grant an exception; no GPU if it sits mostly idle

Batch: a Job

  • Runs your script to the end, then gives the GPU back
  • Submit many at once; the rest wait in Pending for a free GPU
$ kubectl apply -f sweep/        # six training jobs

Six jobs on four GPUs: two wait in Pending and take the first GPUs that free up. When the last one ends, all four GPUs are free again.

A GPU Job

apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata: {name: gpu-train-daniel, namespace: my-lab}     # (1)spec:  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: train        image: pytorch/pytorch:2.9.0-cuda13.0-cudnn9-runtime  # (2)        command: ["python", "train.py"]        resources:                                       # (3)          requests: {cpu: "2", memory: 6Gi, nvidia.com/gpu: 1}          limits:   {cpu: "2", memory: 6Gi, nvidia.com/gpu: 1}      affinity:                                          # (4)        nodeAffinity:          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:            nodeSelectorTerms:            - matchExpressions:              - {key: nvidia.com/gpu.memory, operator: Gt, values: ["20000"]}              - {key: nvidia.com/gpu.compute.major, operator: Gt, values: ["7"]}

(1) Where: your namespace

(2) What: a container image, and the command to run

(3) Resources: 2 CPUs, 6 GB of memory, one GPU

(4) Which GPU: more than 20 GB, Ampere or newer; or name exact models

Where to Start

Use it

  • The LLM API in your automation: config review, log triage, a docs assistant; task names keep working as the catalog changes
  • Your tools in a namespace: web apps, Postgres and ClickHouse from the operators, S3 for data
  • GitLab CI to build and ship them
  • GPUs for AI and ML: a notebook to start, Jobs when it's real

Connect to it

  • Contribute nodes, the way a node joins: you keep priority, NRP runs them
  • InterLink: a Slurm cluster appears as a virtual node
  • Federation with another Kubernetes cluster
  • FABRIC and SENSE testbeds, with Multus for extra NICs
  • perfSONAR: a testpoint on your node joins the mesh
https://nrp.ai/documentation/admindocs/participating/new-contributor-guide/

47

Using GPUs Fairly

Do

  • Run batch work as a Job that exits
  • Request what you'll use; keep limits within 20% of requests
  • Keep data on a persistent volume or in S3
  • Run a sweep as many one-GPU jobs
  • Borrow idle A100/H100s with priorityClassName: opportunistic, and checkpoint

Don't

  • Leave a notebook holding a GPU overnight
  • Put sleep in a Job to keep a GPU (bannable)
  • Ask for 4 GPUs "just in case": use must stay above 40%
  • Keep results on the pod's own disk; it vanishes with the pod
https://nrp.ai/documentation/userdocs/start/policies/
